one_line: Retrofit bolt-on vibration, current and temperature sensors onto old machines, kitchens and laundromats, then run the alerts and utilization dashboards for owners who have no reliability engineer.

problem.summary: Small independent operators run aging equipment with no instrumentation: a machine, walk-in cooler, compressor or fryer fails, nobody knows until product or throughput is already lost, and the fix waits on a parts order. The economics are documented at industry level (downtime cost per hour, share of firms with weekly failures) but almost never measured at the individual 5-200 staff site, because the site has no sensors and no maintenance data. Compliance adds a second, harder deadline in food settings: New Jersey requires refrigerated potentially hazardous food at 41F or below, so an unnoticed cooler drift is both a spoilage event and an inspection finding.

evidence.fact: A NIST analysis of U.S. manufacturing establishments found predictive maintenance was associated with 15% less downtime than preventive maintenance, 87% lower defect rates and 66% less maintenance-related inventory increase; establishments in the top quartile of reactive maintenance had 3.3 times more downtime.

The U.S. DOE Federal Energy Management Program O&M Best Practices Guide (Release 3.0, 2010) states that independent surveys show a functional predictive maintenance program yields 35-45% reduction in downtime, 70-75% elimination of breakdowns, 25-30% lower maintenance costs and 8-12% savings over preventive maintenance alone. These are cited industry averages, not a controlled trial.

MaintainX's 2024 survey of 1,165 maintenance, repair and operations professionals reports the average hour of unplanned downtime at about $25,000, with 29% naming aging equipment as the leading expected cause of unplanned downtime in the next 12 months and 60% citing skilled-trade shortage as the top barrier to improving maintenance.

Parts Town's 'Rethinking Downtime' study, a 2025 survey of roughly 1,800 chain and institutional foodservice respondents, reports 1 in 3 customers experience unplanned equipment downtime every week, with refrigeration and fryers the most frequent and most disruptive failures.

New Jersey retail food rule N.J.A.C. 8:24-1.5 defines refrigeration temperature as 41 degrees Fahrenheit or below, and 8:24-3.2 requires refrigerated potentially hazardous food to be received at 41F or below; a narrow legacy exception for equipment in use before January 2, 2007 ended with a January 2, 2012 upgrade requirement.

Siemens' True Cost of Downtime 2024 puts the high end of unplanned downtime cost for SME manufacturers at about $150,000 per hour, against $2.3 million per hour in automotive; the report also says unplanned downtime costs the world's 500 biggest companies 11% of revenues.

New Jersey's 2023 OEWS estimate for Maintenance and Repair Workers, General (SOC 49-9071) in the Middlesex-Monmouth-Ocean area is $52,326 per year median, roughly $25.16/hour - the labor cost an owner pays for the person who would otherwise walk the floor with a clipboard.

A survey-based study on prognostics and health management reports that only 14% of surveyed small and medium enterprises used predictive maintenance, citing feasibility, cost-effectiveness and value as the considerations.
evidence.year: 2023 (journal publication; survey year not stated in accessible text)

buyers.business_type: Small and mid-size manufacturers - metal fabrication, plastics, food and bakery, pharma/chemical packaging, machine shops

buyers.why: Middlesex County has 824 manufacturing establishments with 30,862 employees (2024 QCEW). Downtime on a single CNC, press, compressor or chiller stops revenue immediately, and these plants usually have one or two maintenance techs rather than a reliability engineer.

gap_for_local_installer: Every named vendor sells a subscription plus sensors to a plant that is assumed to have someone who will act on the alert. A 15-person job shop, a two-location pizza operator and a 60-machine laundromat do not: they have no reliability engineer, no asset register, no baseline and no maintenance calendar, and the vendor's onboarding stops at 'sensor shipped'. The local installer's product is the missing middle: a two-day asset survey and nameplate inventory, per-asset baselining across real load states, per-machine thresholds rather than generic defaults, alert routing to the one person who can actually call the repair tech, and a monthly review that turns the data into a decision (repair, replace, or stop worrying). Three further local wedges: (1) refrigeration temperature plus 41F compliance logging for kitchens, which no vibration vendor sells; (2) utilization dashboards for laundromats and multi-site restaurant groups where the buyer cares about cycles and turns, not bearing frequencies; (3) coordination with the trades - licensed electrician for CT installs, the existing HVAC or kitchen-equipment contractor for the repair - which remote SaaS vendors cannot do.

technical_approach.established_pattern: Four layers. (1) Sensing: bolt-on triaxial vibration + surface temperature on the drive end / non-drive end of each critical rotating asset, sampled periodically (e.g. 1-15 minute intervals, short high-rate bursts for FFT); split-core CT current sensing on the machine's feeder for run/stop, duty cycle and utilization; temperature probes on refrigeration and hot-holding. (2) Transport: LoRaWAN or Wi-Fi to a gateway, then MQTT into a local broker. (3) Analysis: physics-first features (RMS velocity, acceleration, kurtosis, crest factor, envelope demodulation for bearing tones) compared against ISO 20816-style bands and a per-asset learned baseline; time-series storage plus simple anomaly models (z-score/EWMA on RMS, IsolationForest for multi-feature) before any deep learning. (4) Action: rules in Home Assistant or Node-RED, SMS/WhatsApp/email escalation, Grafana or a small web dashboard, and a weekly PDF. Vision is a secondary channel used only where electrical access is impossible or where the question is about state, not condition: Frigate + a YOLO detector for run/stop or cycle counting, and a small VLM for exceptions such as reading an HMI fault screen or a dial thermometer from a still image.

models_and_tools.name: YOLO (Ultralytics YOLOv8/YOLO11, e.g. yolov8n / YOLOv6n)
models_and_tools.role: Object detection for machine/part/operator presence, cycle counting and zone rules; Frigate's default detector model is YOLOv6n. Licence matters: AGPL-3.0 by default, with a paid Enterprise Licence needed to keep a proprietary deployment closed.

models_and_tools.name: Frigate NVR
models_and_tools.role: Camera ingest, motion gating, object detection, zone definitions and MQTT event publishing; runs as Docker or a Home Assistant app and is the pragmatic glue for any camera-based utilization signal.

models_and_tools.name: Home Assistant
models_and_tools.role: Rules engine, notification routing, local dashboards and MQTT consumer; keeps the alerting logic on the customer's site instead of in a vendor cloud.

models_and_tools.name: Liquid AI LFM2.5-VL (450M / 1.6B / 3B)
models_and_tools.role: Small vision-language model for exception explanation on still frames - read a fault code or gauge, describe what changed in a before/after image, classify an unusual scene the rule engine cannot. 3B uses an LFM2.5 backbone with a SigLIP2 400M NaFlex vision encoder; small sizes allow on-box inference.

models_and_tools.name: Qwen3-VL 2B / 4B
models_and_tools.role: Alternative small VLM for HMI/display reading and document-style extraction from panel screens; both sizes are listed as edge-deployable targets (TensorRT Edge-LLM supports 4B, Qualcomm AI Hub lists 2B).

models_and_tools.name: Cactus (Cactus Compute)
models_and_tools.role: On-device inference framework for the phone app a technician uses to photograph nameplates, capture a gauge reading offline and queue uploads; keeps photos of the customer's plant off third-party clouds when required.

models_and_tools.name: llama.cpp
models_and_tools.role: Local runtime for the VLM/LLM layer on a mini PC when the site has no GPU; avoids per-image API cost for continuous camera work.

models_and_tools.name: ISO 20816 vibration severity bands + envelope demodulation
models_and_tools.role: Physics-based thresholds before any ML: overall velocity RMS against machine-class bands, plus bearing-tone envelope analysis. This is what makes a 40-year-old lathe monitorable without a training dataset.

models_and_tools.name: Non-intrusive load monitoring (NILM) / current-signature analysis
models_and_tools.role: Deriving machine on/off and duty cycle from a panel-level CT, and using motor current spectrum for fault screening. Useful when per-machine CTs are too expensive; treat as screening, not diagnosis.

technical_approach.fine_tuning_needed: Mostly no. Vibration and current thresholds are physics-based (ISO 20816 bands, motor nameplate FLA) and need calibration - 2-6 weeks of baseline per asset across its real load states - not model training. A generic anomaly model (z-score/EWMA or IsolationForest on RMS, kurtosis and temperature) is enough for a first pilot and is far more debuggable than a neural net. Fine-tuning or at minimum prompt/example tuning does become necessary for the vision path: reading a specific HMI, gauge or dial is a per-customer visual task, and a few hundred labelled stills per camera plus a LoRA on a 2-4B VLM is the realistic route. Do not fine-tune before you have baselines and a labelled failure history - most small sites have zero recorded failures to train on.
technical_approach.data_needed: Asset register with nameplate data (model, serial, kW/hp, RPM, voltage, service factor) built by walking the floor; 2-6 weeks of continuous baseline at normal operation including startup, idle, full load and shift changes; maintenance and repair history for the last 12-24 months (invoices from the service contractor are usually the only record); failure modes and their consequence cost per asset (scrap, spoilage, lost covers, overtime); for refrigeration, the cold-holding log and any past inspection findings; for the vision path, 200-500 labelled still frames per camera per state (running, stopped, faulted, empty, loaded) and, where available, screen recordings of the HMI.

In factory vibration data covering 11 bearing-failure cases over four years, degradation speed varied widely - some faults developed over months, one became detectable only days before bearing replacement. This is the honest counterweight to 'you always get weeks of warning'.

legal_privacy.rule_or_precedent: New Jersey's Wiretap Act, N.J.S.A. 2A:156A-4, is one-party consent: a participant may record, but a device left running to capture conversations you are not part of is not covered by the exception, and consent obtained for the purpose of committing a crime, tort or other injurious act is excluded. Practical rule for us: no microphones, ever. Vibration and current sensors avoid the issue entirely.

legal_privacy.issue: Employer notice for video-only surveillance of employees
legal_privacy.rule_or_precedent: Could not confirm any New Jersey statute requiring an employer to post notice of video-only camera surveillance, and OSHA's employer-responsibilities page lists required postings and notices without a camera-surveillance notice requirement. Several other states do require notice (Maine, for example), so this is a state-by-state patchwork and notice is cheap insurance.

legal_privacy.issue: Employee monitoring and protected concerted activity
legal_privacy.rule_or_precedent: NLRB General Counsel Memorandum GC 23-02 (Oct 31, 2022) argued that surveillance or algorithmic management tending to deter Section 7 activity can violate the NLRA. The NLRB's own memo index shows GC 23-02 was rescinded on February 14, 2025, so it is no longer current enforcement policy - but the underlying NLRA theory was never overturned and the practical advice (monitor machines, not people; disclose what you collect) still holds.

legal_privacy.issue: State consumer privacy law coverage of site data
legal_privacy.rule_or_precedent: The New Jersey Data Privacy Act (P.L. 2023, c.266) took effect January 15, 2025 and applies at 100,000 consumers, or 25,000 consumers plus revenue from selling personal data; there is no small-business exemption. The Division of Consumer Affairs FAQ indicates employment and job-applicant data sit outside the consumer definition. Machine vibration/current data is not personal data; camera video of identifiable customers or staff is, so that is the part to keep scope-limited.

I could not confirm any New Jersey BIPA-style statute requiring employer consent before collecting employee biometrics. Two premises-facing bills are pending, not law: A3929/S1464 (facial or other remote biometric recognition on consumers at a physical premises, with clear and conspicuous notice, passed the Assembly March 23, 2026 and was referred to a Senate committee May 4, 2026) and S1463 (biometric identifier notice at common entryways, introduced January 13, 2026). Recommendation: no face recognition in any offering.

legal_privacy.issue: Who may install current transformers inside an electrical panel
legal_privacy.rule_or_precedent: N.J.A.C. 13:31-3.8 requires a licensed electrical contractor holding a business permit for installing, maintaining or servicing premises wiring; the Board's FAQ points to N.J.S.A. 45:5A-18 for the narrow exemptions. Any CT or DIN-rail meter work must be subcontracted to a licensed New Jersey electrical contractor, with permit and inspection as the local construction office requires. Battery-powered bolt-on vibration sensors avoid this entirely - a strong reason to lead with them.

legal_privacy.issue: Marketing claims about AI accuracy or savings
legal_privacy.rule_or_precedent: FTC guidance ('Keep your AI claims in check', 2023) applies ordinary truth-in-advertising standards to AI: performance claims, including accuracy, time savings and outperforming alternatives, must be substantiated, and 'AI-powered' is not treated as harmless puffery. For us this means quoting the NIST 15% and the DOE range with their caveats attached, and never promising a percentage of downtime reduction.

legal_privacy.issue: Workplace privacy tort exposure for camera placement
legal_privacy.rule_or_precedent: Hennessey v. Coastal Eagle Point Oil Co., 129 N.J. 81 (1992) recognized that employees retain privacy interests that must be balanced against the employer's legitimate business and safety interests; the employer prevailed there because the job was safety-sensitive. It is a balancing test, not a blanket employer right - so no cameras in break rooms, restrooms, locker areas or changing rooms, and document the business justification for every camera.

legal_privacy.issue: Data retention period for site video and sensor data
legal_privacy.rule_or_precedent: Unknown. I found no New Jersey statute or regulation setting a retention limit for private-employer camera footage or machine telemetry. Best practice (inference): 30 days rolling for video, 24 months for sensor time series, and a written retention clause in the contract.

legal_privacy.issue: Permission to attach sensors to leased equipment or leased premises
legal_privacy.rule_or_precedent: Unknown - I did not find a New Jersey-specific rule. Inference: most commercial leases require landlord consent for attachments or alterations, so the pilot contract should include a landlord/lessor consent line and require reversible, adhesive or clamp mounting.

public: Google/Yelp reviews that name a specific failure: 'machine was out of order', 'cooler broke', 'closed early', 'waited a week for a part' - a review is public evidence of a downtime event the owner already knows about.

Local health department retail food inspection reports showing repeated cold-holding or thermometer violations. New Jersey has no single statewide public inspection database; reports are published by county or municipal health departments, so check the Middlesex County Office of Health Services and the specific town's portal.

Job postings for 'maintenance technician', 'reliability engineer' or 'facilities manager' - a site hiring maintenance staff has both a machine population worth monitoring and a person who can act on an alert.
OSHA establishment-specific injury and inspection data (searchable by employer on osha.gov) - a repeat-amputation or machine-guarding history signals aging equipment and stalled maintenance.

Number of locations, years in business ('serving since 19xx' on the site) and photos showing equipment vintage - a 30-year-old business on the same equipment is the best predictor of a retrofit opportunity (inference).
Square footage and machine count from the company's own site, LinkedIn headcount, or a manufacturer directory listing - needed to size the quote before the first call.
Signs of expansion or a second location (new-location announcement, hiring spree) - utilization dashboards become a purchase decision at exactly that moment.
For laundromats: the store's own review stream mentions specific numbered machines or 'half the washers are broken', which is public evidence of an unmonitored fleet.
walk_in: Nameplates: photograph every machine's data plate for vintage, hp/kW and RPM. Pre-1995 controls with no network port are the target, not the disqualifier.
Oil weeping or puddles under gearboxes, gearmotors and hydraulic power units - a leading indicator of a bearing or seal on its way out.
Handwritten 'out of order' signs, a shelf of spare belts and motors, and a maintenance whiteboard or clipboard with downtime tallies - the site is already tracking the problem manually.
Thermometers: dial thermometers in walk-ins with no logger, ice buildup on evaporator coils, or a clipboard temperature log filled in retroactively.

The electrical room: is there 3-phase 208/480, and is there physical space on the DIN rail or panel gutter for CTs? Is the panel labeled? This determines whether the current-sensing option needs an electrician and a permit.
Wi-Fi coverage at the far end of the plant or basement - if it is bad, a LoRaWAN gateway is the answer, and that is a line item to quote on the spot.
Who fixes things: an in-house tech, a named outside contractor, or 'whoever is free'? A named contractor is a partner to coordinate with, not a competitor.
How the owner currently knows a machine is down: 'the operator tells me', 'I walk the floor at 6am', 'the customer complains'. That sentence is the whole sales case.

Ask three questions: What broke last month, and how long was it down? What does a bad week cost you in dollars or lost customers? Do you know what percentage of the time your bottleneck machine is actually running?
In a laundromat: count machines versus out-of-service tags, and watch whether the attendant has any way to know a dryer stopped heating.

pilot.scope: One site, 8-12 critical assets, six weeks. Week 1: walk the floor, build the asset register with nameplate photos, agree the 8-12 assets and the consequence cost of each failing. Week 2: install sensors, pull 12-24 months of repair invoices, set provisional thresholds. Weeks 3-6: monitor, tune thresholds, run a 30-minute weekly review with the owner or maintenance lead, log every alert and its outcome. Deliverable: a one-page baseline (per-asset run-time percentage, alert count, false-alarm count), at least one documented early catch or a documented decision to change a maintenance interval, and a priced recommendation for a full site.
pilot.hardware: Option A (no electrician, fastest): 8-12 battery-powered bolt-on vibration + surface-temperature sensors (Banner QM30VT2 at $320 each, or LoRaWAN triaxial units at $203-$420), one LoRaWAN gateway if Wi-Fi is weak ($690), one mini PC or Raspberry Pi 5 ($95) running the broker, time-series database and Home Assistant. Option B (utilization-first, needs an electrician): 3-6 Shelly Pro 3EM meters at $150.99 each with CTs plus 4-6 temperature probes. Option C (camera only, where there is no electrical access): a Raspberry Pi 5 + Hailo-8L AI Kit ($95 + $70) running Frigate against existing cameras. Most pilots will mix A with a few temperature probes.
pilot.success_metric: Pre-registered, three parts: (1) at least one verified early catch - an alert that led to an inspection finding a real abnormal condition (loose mount, failing bearing, low refrigerant, blocked condenser) that was repaired before failure, with the repair invoice as evidence; or, if no failure occurs in six weeks, a baseline the owner accepts and acts on, such as 'the bottleneck machine runs 41% of scheduled hours and 60% of that loss is changeover'; (2) false-alarm rate below one per site per week by week 6, since alarm fatigue is the failure mode that kills these installs; (3) owner or maintenance lead says they would keep it at the stated monthly price. Do not use 'downtime reduced by X%' as a six-week metric - six weeks is too short to measure that honestly.
pilot.cost_range: $7,000-$18,000 for a six-week pilot at one site, plus $300-$900/month recurring if it continues.
pilot.assumptions: Assumptions behind that range: single site within ~30 minutes of Milltown; 8-12 assets, not a whole plant; battery-powered sensors so no electrical permit needed for phase one; existing Wi-Fi adequate or one gateway covers the site; owner supplies the asset list and two hours a week; hardware at the list prices cited above (sensors $1,600-$3,800, gateway $690, compute $95-$500); 60-100 hours of our labor at $75-$125/hour ($4,500-$12,500) covering survey, install, baselining, threshold tuning, weekly reviews and the report; excludes any licensed electrical work, which is quoted separately by the electrical contractor, and excludes the cost of the repairs the monitoring identifies. Recurring $300-$900/month assumes 8-12 assets at roughly $25-$75 per asset per month, set below the $45/asset commercial benchmark because we are not providing analyst coverage at that level.

fit_score.rationale: Demand is well documented by government and industry data (NIST 15% less downtime, DOE 35-45%, 1 in 3 foodservice sites failing weekly) but the buyer is a small operator who has lived without this data for 30 years, so demand is real yet unformed - 15/20. Local buyers exist in volume: 824 manufacturing establishments, 1,752 accommodation and food service establishments and 1,710 other-services establishments in Middlesex County in 2024, though only a slice of each has 10+ critical machines - 12/15. Ability to pay is the weak point: a 15-person job shop or a two-location restaurant compares every quote to a $45/asset/month national bundle and to doing nothing - 9/15. Technical feasibility is high: commodity sensors, mature open-source (Frigate, Home Assistant, llama.cpp), physics-based thresholds that need calibration rather than training, and a clear path to a small VLM only for the exception cases - 17/20. Legal risk is low if we stay away from audio and face recognition and subcontract panel work to a licensed electrician; residual risk is alert-driven discipline of an employee and privacy tort exposure from camera placement - 12/15. Defensibility is the real weakness: the hardware is a commodity with published prices and the SaaS vendors are moving downmarket, so the moat is only local presence, per-asset calibration, trade coordination and the owner's trust - 7/15. Total 72/100: a solid, buildable service with a thin margin story, best entered through refrigeration compliance and utilization dashboards rather than competing head-on with vibration-analytics SaaS.

risks: Alert fatigue: a generic threshold that fires on every shift change destroys trust in week two and the owner cancels. This is the most common failure mode and the reason per-asset baselining is the actual product.

Price anchoring from national bundles: MachineCDN publishes $45/asset/month including hardware, LoRaWAN connectivity and software, which leaves little room for a local service margin unless we sell installation, calibration and interpretation as a separate line.
The owner has no maintenance process to receive the alert. Monitoring without a named person and a repair path produces a dashboard nobody opens.
CT and panel work requires a New Jersey licensed electrical contractor (N.J.A.C. 13:31-3.8), adding cost, schedule and a dependency we do not control.
Hardware longevity in real kitchens and plants: washdown, heat, grease and vibration kill consumer-grade sensors; a 5-year battery claim is a vendor claim, not a field-verified number.

Liability if we miss a failure: a spoilage event or a stopped line after we installed 'monitoring' invites a claim that we assumed a duty of care. Contract language must state that the system is advisory, not a guarantee, and cap liability.
Licensing: Ultralytics YOLO is AGPL-3.0 by default and its models trained with its code are covered; shipping it inside a closed appliance needs the paid Enterprise Licence or a different detector.
Cybersecurity and network politics: putting any device on a small manufacturer's flat network, or asking for IT cooperation they do not have, can stall an install for weeks.

No failure history to train on: small sites often have zero recorded failures, so any 'predictive' claim beyond threshold trending is unsupported - sell condition monitoring and utilization, not failure prediction.
Scalability of the service model: 8-12 asset installs and weekly reviews do not scale past a handful of sites per technician without heavy templating and remote triage.
caveats: Three things to hold lightly. First, the headline savings numbers are not from businesses like the ones we would serve: NIST's 15% is an establishment-level association, DOE's 35-45% is a decades-old aggregate of unnamed 'independent surveys', and Siemens' $150,000/hour is the top end of SME manufacturing - none of them is a controlled trial at a 20-person job shop. Second, most of the concrete case studies with attractive numbers (Emerson/Johns Manville 260% ROI, Augury's <6-month payback, Waites' $11M save) are vendor marketing, rated Low here, and should never be repeated to a prospect as an expectation. Third, the honest technical picture from the peer-reviewed vibration literature is that warning lead time varies from months to days depending on the fault, so a pilot should promise detection and a baseline, not advance warning. Middlesex County counts are sector-level (824 manufacturing, 1,752 food service, 1,710 other services establishments, 2024 QCEW) and include employers far outside the 5-200 staff band; the addressable subset is smaller and unmeasured.
data_gaps: No laundromat-specific study quantifying revenue lost per machine-hour of downtime was found. The Coin Laundry Association white paper on equipment replacement was retrieved but did not yield extractable dollar figures in this pass, and the American Laundry News maintenance survey page returned HTTP 403. The laundromat case rests on inference from per-cycle revenue, not on a citable loss study.

No statewide New Jersey public retail food inspection database exists; reports are published by county and municipal health departments, so inspection-history prospecting needs a per-town list that was not built here.

Two vendor prices (VibeCloud at roughly $26/sensor/month and Chladni at $79/machine/month) appeared only in a search-result summary and were not opened on the vendor's own page, so they were left out of existing_solutions rather than cited unverified.

The MDPI factory vibration dataset page returned HTTP 403 on direct fetch; the 11-case/four-year description and the 'days to months' lead-time finding come from the search result summary of that page, not from reading the paper.

BLS OEWS county-level detail could not be pulled directly (the county table did not render); the $52,326 figure is the 2023 Middlesex-Monmouth-Ocean area estimate from a New Jersey Department of Labor PDF, not a Middlesex-only figure.

Census County Business Patterns establishment counts by employment-size band for Middlesex County could not be retrieved (the Census API response was not extractable), so the share of local establishments in the 5-200 staff band remains an estimate from a third-party aggregator and is not cited.
No measured outcome was found for camera-based utilization monitoring deployed in a real laundromat, restaurant or job shop - the vision accuracy numbers available are lab or single-study results.
Fine-tuning costs and the price of a used industrial mini PC were not established from primary sources; both are marked Unknown in hardware rather than estimated.
Whether any New Jersey rule requires employer notice for video-only surveillance, or sets a video retention limit, could not be confirmed in either direction.
